title: AI, jobs and prices: what euro area consumers expect
author: European Central Bank
text:
THE ECB BLOGAI, jobs and prices: what euro area consumers expect27 November 2026By Dimitris Georgarakos, Geoff Kenny and Justus MeyerArtificial intelligence could significantly boost productivity, but its effects on prices will depend on how quickly it is adopted and how consumers respond. New evidence from the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey sheds light on consumers’ views on jobs, prices and AI regulation.[1] This blog draws on ongoing research conducted as part of the ECB Research Task Force’s work on the economic effects of AI, including Workstream A on AI and the real economy. The work presented here forms part of a forthcoming working paper: Borlescu, A., Georgarakos, D., Kenny, G., Pairan, T. and Meyer, J. (2026), “AI diffusion in the euro area: Adoption, workplace effects and economic expectations”, mimeo, European Central Bank. The authors thank the ECB’s CES team for collecting and processing the data and Ipsos for carrying out the survey. Overall adoption rates of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace have increased substantially, as AI has moved rapidly from experimentation to regular use. More than 50% of workers reported using AI at work in May 2026.[2] See Lane, P. R. (2026), “AI adoption in Europe”, keynote speech at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy, San Francisco, 30 October. In August 2026, 44% of employed euro area consumers reported using AI at least weekly at work, and around 18% used it daily. Many AI users report that the technology already helps them produce more or higher-quality work, and workers expect its use to broaden substantially over the next five years.However, widespread adoption does not automatically translate into economy-wide productivity gains. Firms also need to invest in skills, data, computing capacity and organisational change, while consumers need to adapt their behaviour. New evidence from the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey (CES)[3] For background on the CES, see ECB (2021), “ECB Consumer Expectations Survey: an overview and first evaluation”, Occasional Paper Series, No 287, and Georgarakos, D. and G. Kenny (2022), “Household Spending and Fiscal Support During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Insights from a New Consumer Survey”, 129(2022), Journal of Monetary Economics, S1-S14. shows how consumers see this transition in real time, and what they expect it to mean for productivity, jobs and prices.Rapid AI adoption, despite weaker investmentDaily AI use has increased steadily over the past year (Chart 1, panel a). Overall, AI adoption in the euro area is similar to that in the United States. Strikingly, a larger share of consumers in the euro area report using AI daily, although this gap is narrowing.Chart 1AI adoption is rising, but barriers remaina) AI adoption in the euro area and the United States b) Barriers to AI use(percentage of consumers, by region)(percentage of employed consumers not using AI)Sources: CES, authors’ calculations and Gallup. Notes: Panel a): euro area estimates are population-weighted CES estimates among employed consumers aged 18-64, latest data from August 2026. United States estimates are from Gallup (latest data: August 2026). Importantly, CES and Gallup use different survey questions and samples, so comparisons across regions should be interpreted as indicative of trends rather than fully harmonised estimates. In Gallup, total AI users includes employees who say they use AI daily, a few times a week, a few times a month or a few times a year. In the CES, every May, as part of a special module on labour market topics employed consumers are asked if they personally use artificial intelligence (AI) in their work. Daily use of AI is collected in the CES at irregular frequency since June 2025 (latest data: August 2025) by asking respondents about the frequency of their AI use for tasks related to their job. Panel b): population-weighted shares among employed respondents aged 18-64 who reported not using AI at work in June 2025. Respondents could select multiple barriers. EA-11 denotes the population-weighted average across the 11 euro area countries covered by the CES.Rapid adoption, however, does not necessarily translate into domestic investment. A recent estimate projects that investments by firms will rise by around 40% in the United States between 2021 and the end of 2027, compared with about 12% in the euro area, with AI-related investment contributing significantly to US growth.[4] See also Financial Times (2026), “US widens AI-driven investment gap with Europe”, 24 August. See also for a more comprehensive analysis Andersson, M., Jarvis, V. and Soudan, M. (2025), “Business investment: why is the euro area lagging behind the United States?”, ECB Economic Bulletin, Issue 2/2025, European Central Bank. Combined with high and rising AI adoption, weaker domestic investment could also increase Europe’s dependence on foreign AI-related technologies and infrastructure. At the same time, many workers still face barriers to using AI at work, and daily use remains limited. These barriers are similar across the largest euro area economies (Chart 1, panel b). Skills and knowledge gaps, together with privacy and security concerns, are among the most frequently reported obstacles. By contrast, social norms and existing regulations are less frequently identified as direct barriers.For policymakers, the similarity of barriers across the euro area suggests that euro area wide measures could support wider AI adoption, including training to address skills gaps, clear employer policies on safe AI use and better access to approved tools. The prominence of privacy concerns also indicates that trusted, appropriately governed AI tools, such as European solutions, could encourage wider workplace adoption.Policy efforts can support AI diffusion in several ways. Safeguards can build confidence among workers and consumers, while clear and predictable rules can make it easier for firms to invest in and deploy AI. The challenge for Europe is to combine these objectives by supporting trusted use without creating unnecessary complexity or uncertainty that could deter investment.What happens once AI is actually incorporated into work?According to recent CES findings, consumers report that AI helps them save time. But time savings alone do not necessarily increase productivity. For AI to expand effective capacity, workers need to translate faster task completion into more or better-quality output.The CES shows that workplace AI users report perceived gains in both the quantity and quality of their work (Chart 2, panel a). Around 56% say that AI increases the amount of work they complete, while 47% report producing higher-quality output. Among those indicating that they complete more work, 62% cite AI’s ability to help them find or process information, and 51% say that it reduces the effort required to perform their work. Other frequently reported benefits include generating new ideas, automating repetitive tasks and handling larger workloads. However, these perceived gains are not universal. Among users who reported no increase in output, the most commonly cited reason is the time needed to check or correct AI-generated results (Chart 2, panel b). Other reported obstacles include AI not being suitable for the task and concerns about retaining control. This points to remaining workplace frictions at the task-level and suggests that productivity gains depend on the tasks for which AI is used and the degree of verification and human oversight required.[5] The aggregation problem is central to macroeconomic assessments of AI. Economy-wide productivity depends not only on how much AI improves the tasks it performs well, but also on the share of those tasks in total work, the pace of adoption and the complementary organisational changes required. See Acemoglu, D. (2025), “Institutions, Technology and Prosperity”, Economic Policy, Vol 40, No 121, and Brynjolfsson, E., Syverson, C. and Rock, D. (2021), “The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies”, American Economic Journal, Vol 13, No 1. See also Dell’Acqua, F. et al. (2026), “Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality”, Organization Science, Vol 37, No 2. As workers learn where AI can be used most effectively and firms adapt their workflows, some of the constraints currently limiting productivity gains may diminish. Translating AI use into higher productivity is likely to be a gradual process of experimentation and adjustment.Chart 2Perceived effects of AI on productivitya) Effects on work quantity and qualityb) How AI affects the amount of work completed(percentage of AI users, employed consumers)(percentage of AI users, employed consumers)Sources: CES and authors’ calculations.Notes: Panel a) shows population-weighted shares among employed respondents aged 18-64, including employees and the self-employed, who reported using AI at work in June 2026. Respondents were asked separately whether AI had changed the amount of work they completed and the quality of their work. Panel b) shows population-weighted shares among employed respondents aged 18-64 who reported using AI at work. “Helpful” refers to users who reported that AI increased the amount of work completed; “not more helpful” refers to users who reported either no change or a decrease. Respondents could select multiple reasons.Broader use brings opportunities and adjustment costsWorkers increasingly expect the use of AI to become more widespread. In August 2026, employed respondents aged 18-64 expected 46% of workers in their current sector to use AI within five years, up from 34% one year earlier (Chart 3, panel a). This upward revision is visible across the distribution, not just among the most optimistic respondents. The pace at which AI spreads also matters because households and firms often base their decisions on what they expect will happen. Higher productivity and incomes could support spending and investment. At the same time, concerns about jobs and wages could make workers more cautious about their current employment situation and more inclined to consider alternative job opportunities.AI can therefore affect the economy through two channels: the productivity gains it eventually delivers and the expectations it creates along the way. Both can influence spending, saving, investment, labour market choices and, ultimately, prices.The CES points to both opportunities and adjustment costs (Chart 3, panel b). Around half of respondents expect AI to save time on everyday tasks or make it easier to find the best prices for goods and services, while many also expect to gain access to better products and services.Chart 3Expected adoption and near-term effects of AIa) Expected AI use at work over the next five yearsb) Expected effects of AI over the next 12 months(percentage of employed consumers)(percentage of employed consumers)Sources: CES and authors’ calculations.Notes: Panel a) shows population-weighted estimates among employed respondents aged 18-64 of the expected share of workers in their sector who will use AI over the next five years. Dashed vertical lines indicate the survey means. Panel b) shows population-weighted shares of employed respondents aged 18-64 who expect each effect over the next 12 months, based on the June 2026 survey. Outcomes were measured separately, so the shares do not sum to 100%.At the same time, consumers expect AI to bring not only benefits but also some costs. Learning new skills and spending more time checking information are among the challenges they anticipate. Consumers are more likely to see AI as increasing the risk of job loss than as raising household income or improving job opportunities over the next year. A sizeable share also expects AI to push up prices of goods and services over the same period.[6] Among respondents who expect AI to increase prices, greater pricing power for firms and higher energy and material costs are the most cited reasons, according to additional CES data that will be covered in Borlescu et al. (2026). Such perceptions help show how AI may affect the economy during the transition, because households and firms often make spending, saving and investment decisions based on their expectations.Support for AI regulationConsumers’ concerns about AI are also reflected in their views on regulation. Support for safeguards does not simply reflect unfamiliarity with the technology. For instance, demand for AI regulation is strong among both regular AI users and those who use it less often or not at all (Chart 4, panel a). Across euro area countries, support for regulation also tends to be stronger in countries where workers also perceive a greater risk of losing their jobs due to AI (Chart 4, panel b). While this relationship does not establish causality, it suggests that economic insecurity may be one factor shaping attitudes towards AI regulation.Chart 4Consumers’ demand for AI regulationa) Consumers’ demand for AI regulationb) Demand for regulation and perceived AI-related job loss risk(percentage of employed consumers)(country-level averages)Sources: CES and authors’ calculations.Notes: In August 2026 consumers were asked whether priority should be given to “the development of AI, even if this means accepting greater risks” or “regulating AI, even if this slows its development”. Panel a) shows the population-weighted average demand for AI regulation among employed respondents, by AI use frequency. Demand for regulation is measured on a scale from 1 to 7, with higher values indicating stronger support. Panel b) shows population-weighted averages by country among employed respondents in August 2026. The horizontal axis reports the average subjective probability of losing one’s current job because of AI, while the vertical axis reports average demand for regulation. The fitted line shows an unweighted linear relationship across countries, with each country given equal weight. The relationship is descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal.The CES findings point to a delicate balance. Consumers see clear benefits from AI, but they also worry about jobs, privacy, security and the reliability of AI-generated information. Clear rules on data use and accountability, together with access to trusted tools and the skills needed to use them, can help build confidence. The challenge for Europe is to put those safeguards in place without unnecessarily slowing the investment and innovation needed to realise AI’s productivity potential.The views expressed in each blog entry are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem.Check out The ECB Blog and subscribe for future posts.For topics relating to banking supervision, why not have a look at The Supervision Blog?
